## Worldview
Medicine follows Galen and Avicenna as taught at Bologna, Padua and Montpellier: disease is an imbalance of the four humours; pestilence comes from corrupted air (miasma) stirred up by planetary conjunctions, earthquakes and God's anger at sin. Natural philosophy is scholastic Aristotle. Astrology is respected science. There is no printing: knowledge travels by sermon, council decree, notary, letter and copyist, and most people cannot read Latin. Florence is a guild republic of perhaps 90,000 to 100,000 people, governed since 1343 by priors drawn by lot from the guilds, shaken by the collapse of the Bardi and Peruzzi banks and by the famine of 1346–47. The pope sits at Avignon. Practical knowledge lives in workshops and guilds; merchants reckon with Arabic numerals in abacus schools but keep formal ledgers in Roman numerals.

## People
- **Gentile da Foligno**: Professor of medicine at Perugia, the most respected physician in central Italy. Knows: Avicenna's Canon; writes plague consilia for Genoa (late 1347 or early 1348), Perugia and Pisa (poisonous corrupted air, contagion, theriac, bleeding, fires, avoidance of the sick). — At Perugia in 1347, three or four days' ride from Florence. Dies of plague near Foligno on 18 June 1348 after tending the sick.
- **Tommaso del Garbo**: Florentine physician, son of the physician Dino del Garbo; professor at Perugia and Bologna. Knows: Galenic and Avicennan medicine; author of a vernacular Consiglio contro a pistolenza with practical household advice (airing rooms, vinegar, keeping distance from the sick). — Where he is in autumn 1347 is not certain (Florence, Perugia or Bologna). Survives the plague; dies 1370.
- **Giovanni Villani**: Merchant, former mint and grain official, chronicler. Knows: The city's numbers (baptisms, mouths, schools, hospitals, wool output), the 1333 flood, the famine of 1346–47, the bank failures, astrology of calamities. — In Florence, ruined by the Buonaccorsi failure and jailed for it in the Stinche in 1346. Dies in the plague in 1348, leaving the chronicle unfinished.
- **Matteo Villani**: Giovanni's brother, merchant. Knows: Commerce and city politics; continues the chronicle and describes the plague and its aftermath. — In Florence; survives 1348 and dies in the plague of 1363.
- **Giovanni Boccaccio**: Writer, son of the merchant Boccaccino di Chellino. Knows: Naples and its court, Latin letters, the merchant world; later describes the plague in Florence in the Decameron. — Probably at Forlì or Ravenna in 1347; whether he witnessed the Florentine plague himself is debated. His father dies in 1349.
- **Guy de Chauliac**: Surgeon and physician to Pope Clement VI. Knows: Surgery, anatomy from Bologna and Montpellier; in 1348 distinguishes a first form with fever and blood-spitting from a later form with buboes. — At Avignon. Stays at his post in 1348, falls ill with a bubo and survives.
- **Angelo Acciaiuoli**: Dominican, bishop of Florence (1342–1355). Knows: The clergy, preaching and processions, which are how instructions reach the whole city without print. — In Florence; a leader of the 1343 rising against the Duke of Athens. Survives the plague.
- **Francesco Balducci Pegolotti**: Former factor of the Bardi company, author of the merchant handbook Pratica della mercatura. Knows: Trade routes to Tana and Cathay, spices, alum, soap, sugar grades, assaying and refining of gold and silver. — In Florence in 1347, occupied with the liquidation of the Bardi company. Date of death unknown.
- **Paolo dell'Abbaco (Paolo Dagomari)**: abacus master, astronomer and astrologer. Knows: commercial arithmetic, algebra in words, root extraction, astronomical tables and almanacs. — About 65, teaches at his school by Santa Trinita in Florence; the best-known reckoner in the city. Survives the plague and dies in 1374.
- **Jacopo Dondi**: physician and astronomer in Padua. Knows: the astronomical tower clock set up in Padua in 1344, astronomical tables, tides. — In Padua, about a week's journey from Florence. Dies in 1359.
- **Giovanni Dondi**: student of medicine and astronomy, Jacopo's son. Knows: clockwork and planetary theory; begins his astrarium, a geared planetary clock, in 1348. — About seventeen, in Padua. Survives the plague; finishes the astrarium in 1364.
- **Jean Buridan**: master of arts at the university of Paris. Knows: impetus, logic of consequences, questions on Aristotle's physics. — In Paris, weeks away; reachable by letter in Latin through friars or merchants. Survives the plague.
- **Thomas Bradwardine**: Oxford mathematician and theologian, royal chaplain. Knows: proportions of speeds, the Merton school's arithmetic of motion. — With Edward III in France and England. Becomes archbishop of Canterbury in 1349 and dies of the plague that August.
- **Jean de Murs**: astronomer, mathematician and music theorist in Paris. Knows: Alfonsine Tables, eclipse computation, calendar reform, arithmetic and algebra. — In Paris; advised Clement VI at Avignon on the calendar in 1344-1345. Alive into the 1350s.
- **Andrea Pisano**: sculptor, goldsmith and master builder. Knows: bronze door casting, the campanile works, stone hoisting. — Made the Baptistery's bronze doors (1330-1336); by 1347 master of works at Orvieto cathedral. Dies about 1348-1349.
- **Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch)**: poet and scholar, crowned in Rome 1341, son of a Florentine exile. Knows: Cicero, Livy, manuscript hunting, the papal court. — At Avignon and Vaucluse until November 1347, then Parma and Verona. Has never lived in Florence (first visit 1350). Survives; his Laura dies at Avignon in April 1348.
- **Clement VI (Pierre Roger)**: pope at Avignon since 1342. Knows: theology, diplomacy, patronage of scholars and physicians. — At Avignon, some weeks' journey away. In July and September 1348 issues bulls forbidding attacks on Jews over the plague. Survives.
- **Bartolus of Sassoferrato**: professor of civil law. Knows: Roman law, city statutes, the legal standing of free cities. — Teaching at Perugia since 1343. Survives the plague; dies 1357.
- **Werner of Urslingen**: German mercenary captain, leader of the Great Company. Knows: cavalry warfare, extortion by contract. — Plundered Tuscany in 1342; in 1347–48 serves Louis of Hungary's invasion of Naples.
- **Cola di Rienzo**: notary, tribune of Rome from May 1347. Knows: Roman antiquities and inscriptions, popular oratory. — Rules Rome May–December 1347 and writes to Florence for support; flees in December.

## Events and timeline
- 1346 Jan: the Bardi company fails (January 1345 in Florentine reckoning), after the Peruzzi (1343); credit and employment in the city collapse.
- 1346: plague breaks out in the Mongol army besieging Genoese Caffa in the Crimea.
- 1346 Mar: the Franciscan inquisitor Piero dell'Aquila, collecting a cardinal's debt from the failed Acciaiuoli, has citizens seized; a crowd frees one. He excommunicates the priors and lays an interdict; the commune curbs his powers and the clergy's armed retinues.
- 1346 Aug 26: Crécy. English archers and dismounted men-at-arms defeat French cavalry and Genoese crossbowmen; Villani reports English bombards.
- 1346 Sep–1347 Aug: Edward III besieges Calais for eleven months; it surrenders from hunger.
- 1346 autumn: harvest fails across Tuscany after months of rain.
- 1347 Feb: Genoa founds the Maona of Chios, repaying the shipowners of its 1346 fleet with shares in the island's revenues.
- 1347 Apr: William of Ockham dies at Munich.
- 1347 mid-Apr: famine at its worst. The commune bakes bread in its own ovens and rations it by ticket, two loaves a mouth; Villani counts 94,000 mouths.
- 1347 May 20: Cola di Rienzo seizes power in Rome as tribune; he abdicates and flees on Dec 15.
- 1347 summer: sickness follows the famine; Villani reports more than 4,000 dead in Florence, mostly women and children.
- 1347 Aug: the commune issues a new, worse silver coin, the guelfo of five soldi; a comet is seen, which Villani records as a sign.
- 1347 early Oct: Genoese galleys from the Black Sea bring the plague to Messina.
- 1347 Oct 11: Emperor Ludwig of Bavaria dies excommunicate; the pope's candidate Charles IV is left as king.
- 1347 Oct 23: date of the oldest surviving premium insurance contract, drawn by a Genoese notary.
- 1347 autumn: rumours of the sickness reach Florence with merchants' letters; the commune takes first precautions.
- 1347 Nov: Petrarch leaves Avignon for Italy. Louis of Hungary marches through Italy toward Naples; Queen Joanna flees to Provence.
- 1347 Nov–Dec: plague in Sardinia, Corsica and Marseille.
- 1347 Nov 25: Nicholas of Autrecourt recants and burns his writings in Paris.
- 1348 Jan: plague at Genoa and Pisa (carried to Pisa by galleys), soon after at Venice. Louis of Hungary enters Naples. Jan 25: great earthquake in Friuli and Carinthia, felt across northern Italy and read as a sign; the last event in Villani's chronicle.
- 1348 early: Florence has the streets cleaned, refuses entry to the sick and holds processions (Boccaccio).
- 1348 Mar: first plague deaths in Florence. Mar 30: Venice appoints three citizens as a temporary health commission.
- 1348 Apr: Florence gives a temporary commission of eight citizens special powers over cleaning, removal of the sick and infected goods, and burials.
- 1348 May 2: Pistoia issues plague ordinances: no travel to or from Pisa and Lucca, no imported cloth, deep graves, limits on funerals, rules for butchers.
- 1348 May–Jul: the plague peaks in Florence; perhaps half the city dies. Shops and courts close, the rich flee to their villas, the dead go into layered trench graves (Stefani). Giovanni Villani dies, and the painters Bernardo Daddi in Florence and probably the Lorenzetti brothers in Siena.
- 1348 Jun 9: Queen Joanna sells Avignon to Clement VI.
- 1348 Jun 18: Gentile da Foligno dies of plague near Foligno.
- 1348 Jul 6 and Sep 26: Clement VI's bulls declare the charge that Jews cause the plague false and forbid harming them; massacres nonetheless spread from Provence and Savoy into the Empire that autumn.
- 1348 late summer–autumn: the plague ebbs in Florence. The Company of Orsanmichele is left some 350,000 florins by the dying (Matteo Villani). The commune resolves to found a university (Studio); the papal charter follows in May 1349.
- 1348 Oct: the Paris medical faculty delivers its Compendium de epidemia to King Philip VI: the cause is the conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars in Aquarius on 20 March 1345, corrupting the air.
- 1348: Giovanni Dondi begins the astrarium in Padua (finished 1364).

## Quest hooks
- Ride to Perugia before winter and argue with Gentile da Foligno; his consilium will be copied across Italy, so whatever he writes about clothing, bedding and the sickroom will travel further than any sermon.
- Persuade the priors to make the gate officials hold back cloth, bedding and travellers from Pisa for a fixed number of days, against the wool guild and a city still hungry from the famine.
- Get Giovanni Villani, bankrupt and bitter, and the parish gravediggers to tally deaths by parish and week, the first such count in the city, and keep the tally going if Villani dies himself.
- The grain at Orsanmichele is full of rats. Rat-proofing the stores can be sold to the grain officials as saving bread, with no theory of plague needed.
- A physician reports that patients who cough blood die within three days and so do those who nursed them, while bubo patients' nurses sometimes live. What does the player make of it, and who will listen?
- Without print, an instruction reaches the city only through the bishop's preachers, the guild consuls, notaries and criers. Each channel wants something in return.
- A Dominican preacher will carry any message to thousands, if it can be squared with scripture and Galen.
- Rumours of poisoned wells arrive from across the Alps. Anything the player has said about invisible things in water may be turned against the city's few Jews or against strangers.
- Florence has no public clock. The Signoria would pay for one on the tower of the Palazzo dei Priori; the nearest people who understand an escapement are the Dondi in Padua.
- Paolo dell'Abbaco can turn a rule into a table faster than anyone in the city. Win him and logarithms, decimal fractions or a count of the dead become possible.
- A physician's water-filled urine flask in a sunbeam shows that colours come out of white light. The Dominicans know Theodoric's rainbow and will argue.
- The mint tests florins by touchstone and fire. Weighing a coin in air and in water would catch false gold without destroying it.
- Spectacle makers grind only convex lenses. The first concave pair lets a short-sighted prior or banker see across the piazza.
- For the Baptistery doors Florence had to fetch a founder from Venice. Anything in cast bronze larger than a bell needs outside help or patient trials.
- A letter to Buridan in Paris on falling and thrown bodies would reach the one man in Europe already halfway there.
- Creditors of a failed company fight over ledgers at the Mercanzia; an honest reckoning would be worth a patron.
- A merchant back from Caffa or Tana tells what he saw of the sickness in the East.
- The grain officials must feed 94,000 mouths again and suspect the bakers' count.
- Holders of Monte credits want to know what a promise of the commune is worth.
- The commune hears a free company is coming south with the Hungarian army and must choose between paying it off and manning the walls.
- A cartolaio with ten copyists cannot fill an order; he would listen to any way of making books faster.
- A journey to Avignon to reach Clement VI's court before the plague does.
- A copy of the Florentine merchants' letter from Seville about the Canaries voyage of 1341, which Boccaccio put into Latin, is passed round; it tells of islands out in the Ocean.

## Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/medicine.md)
- `anatomy_dissection` (Human anatomy from dissection): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Bologna teaches from Mondino's Anathomia (1316), which mostly confirms Galen. Florence has no anatomy teaching; legal post-mortems, as at Bologna in 1302, are rare but known. Local: physicians of the Arte dei Medici e Speziali; Santa Maria Nuova. Elsewhere: Bologna and Padua, anatomy teaching on executed criminals; Paris, Guido da Vigevano's illustrated Anathomia (1345).
- `childbirth_care` (Safe childbirth (clean hands, patience, cord care, forceps)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:low. Midwives and female relatives attend births at home; physicians stay out. Turning the child is in the Arabic authors. No forceps. Local: midwives; Ospedale di San Gallo and Santa Maria della Scala (foundlings).
- `food_hygiene` (Food hygiene (cooking, flies, carriers)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Officials and the butchers' guild inspect meat and fish by smell and look. Stinking meat counts as a source of corrupt air, so rules tighten in 1348. Local: Mercato Vecchio; butchers' guild (Arte dei Beccai). Elsewhere: Pistoia, ordinances of May 1348 regulate butchers.
- `nursing_hospital_hygiene` (Hospital hygiene and trained nursing): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Villani counts thirty hospitals, over a thousand beds. Santa Maria Nuova nurses with lay sisters, food and linen; beds are shared. The Misericordia carries the sick and buries the dead. Local: Ospedale di Santa Maria Nuova (founded 1288); Compagnia della Misericordia; Ospedale di San Gallo (foundlings); Ospedale di San Paolo. Elsewhere: Cairo, Mansuri hospital with wards by disease; Siena, Santa Maria della Scala.
- `opium_analgesia` (Pain relief with opium and willow bark (laudanum, morphine, aspirin)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Opium is sold mostly inside theriac, the leading plague remedy, at unknown strength; mandrake and henbane too. Willow bark is unused for fever. Dosing is guesswork. Local: apothecaries (speziali); theriac from Venice, Genoa and Montpellier.
- `parasitic_worms` (Parasitic worms (hookworm, roundworm, tapeworm, guinea worm)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Worms are seen and treated with wormseed and bitter herbs. They are thought to breed from rotting humours; eggs, soil and undercooked pork are not suspected. Local: apothecaries (wormseed).
- `wound_care` (Wound care (stop bleeding, clean, tie vessels, leave dirty wounds open)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Surgeons split over pus: Theodoric of Lucca taught clean healing with wine dressings, most still provoke 'laudable pus'. Plague buboes are cut or cauterised. Bleeding is stopped mainly by cautery. Local: surgeons of the Arte dei Medici e Speziali; surgeons at Santa Maria Nuova. Elsewhere: Bologna, surgical tradition of Theodoric and William of Saliceto; Avignon, Guy de Chauliac.
- `sanitation_sewerage` (Latrines and sewers (keeping excrement out of water, food and soil)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Statutes forbid dumping filth in streets. Cesspits leak into wells; dyers, tanners and butchers foul the Arno. In early 1348 the commune has the city cleaned against the stench. Local: cesspit emptiers; Arno; commune's street and market officials.
- `antiseptics` (Antiseptics (strong spirit, chlorinated lime, carbolic acid, iodine)): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Wine and vinegar go on wounds without a theory. Vinegar is the plague year's all-purpose wash for hands, face, coins and rooms. Strong spirit can be made; chlorinated lime cannot. Local: apothecaries; monastery stills.
- `boiled_water` (Boiling drinking water and protecting wells): K2 use:none make:easy acc:medium. Avicenna advises boiling suspect water. Wells and the Arno supply the city. Talk of something unseen in wells can feed poisoning rumours; Jews are murdered on that charge in 1348–49. Elsewhere: China, habitual tea drinking.
- `quarantine` (Quarantine and isolation of the sick): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Lepers are segregated; a waiting period for arrivals exists nowhere yet. In 1348 Florence refuses entry to the sick. Closing gates to goods means hunger after the famine; merchants resist. Local: leper hospital of San Jacopo a Sant'Eusebio outside the walls; city gates and their gabelle officials; Signoria (priors of the guilds). Elsewhere: Pistoia, May 1348 ban on people and cloth from Pisa and Lucca; Milan, Visconti restrictions in 1348; Islamic lands, tradition against entering or leaving a plague land.
- `tuberculosis_control` (Consumption (tuberculosis) is contagious): K2 use:none make:easy acc:low. Avicenna's Canon, the university textbook, lists phthisis as catching, but physicians treat it as a constitution. Families nurse the sick at home.
- `dental_care` (Tooth decay and dental care): K1 use:wrong make:easy acc:medium. Toothache is blamed on a tooth worm, treated with henbane smoke; barbers and travelling tooth-drawers extract. Sugar is a luxury, so decay is moderate.
- `epidemiology_mapping` (Counting and mapping cases to find causes (epidemiology)): K1 use:none make:easy acc:medium. No death registers exist. Giovanni Villani reports baptisms counted with beans at the Baptistery, and counts of mouths, schools and hospital beds. Parishes and gravediggers could supply tallies. Local: Giovanni Villani; Baptistery of San Giovanni (bean count of baptisms); parish priests and gravediggers (beccamorti).
- `contagion_theory` (Contagion by invisible living agents (germ theory)): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Plague is corrupted, poisonous air from conjunctions and rot. Physicians add that the sick 'infect' others by breath and belongings. Varro's tiny animals are in a rare, unread manuscript. Local: Arte dei Medici e Speziali; physicians trained at Bologna. Elsewhere: Perugia, Gentile da Foligno (poisonous vapour reaching heart and lungs); Granada and Almería, Ibn al-Khatib and Ibn Khatima (their contagion tracts follow in 1349 and after).
- `malaria_mosquito` (Malaria carried by mosquitoes (drainage, nets)): K1 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Marsh fevers (tertian, quartan) are blamed on bad air. Avoiding marshes in summer works for the wrong reason. Drainage is costly; fine cloth nets are cheap. Local: Maremma; Pisan plain; Val di Chiana; Padule di Fucecchio.
- `water_filtration_chlorination` (Slow sand filtration and chlorination of town water): K1 use:none make:medium acc:medium. Masons could build a sand filter like the Venetian cisterns. Chlorination is out of reach; no one can make the chemical. Elsewhere: Venice, rainwater cisterns that filter through a bed of sand.
- `clinical_thermometer_stethoscope` (Physical diagnosis (percussion, stethoscope, thermometer, pulse count)): K1 use:none make:hard acc:medium. Physicians judge pulse by touch and inspect urine in a flask; fever is felt by hand. No small timekeeper exists; a sandglass or counted prayers must serve. Local: glassmakers; physicians' uroscopy.
- `bloodletting_harm` (Abandoning bloodletting, purging and mercury (end of humoral medicine)): K0 make:easy acc:low. Bleeding, purging and cupping are standard, also as plague prevention; the plague consilia of 1348 prescribe them. Patients expect it and barbers live from it. Local: Arte dei Medici e Speziali; barbers who perform bloodletting.
- `cholera_waterborne` (Cholera and typhoid spread through drinking water): K0 make:easy acc:low. Asiatic cholera does not exist here. Summer fluxes are common, worst after the famine, and blamed on bad food, fruit and air.
- `first_aid_resuscitation` (First aid and resuscitation): K0 make:easy acc:medium. No method exists for reviving the apparently dead. The drowned are hung head down or rolled. A revival may be called a miracle or sorcery.
- `hand_hygiene` (Hand washing with soap): K0 make:easy acc:low. Hands are washed before meals for manners. Soap and basins exist. Washing between patients has no rationale in a medicine of bad air and humours. Local: Arte dei Medici e Speziali; Santa Maria Nuova.
- `heat_sterilisation` (Sterilising instruments and dressings by heat): K0 make:easy acc:medium. Boiling instruments and linen is within any hospital's means. It needs fuel and a new routine; fire is already trusted to purify air.
- `oral_rehydration` (Oral rehydration (water, salt and sugar)): K0 make:easy acc:medium. Salt is taxed and sugar is an apothecary's luxury; honey is the cheap substitute. Physicians restrict drink in fluxes.
- `plague_vectors` (Plague carried by rats and fleas (and by coughing)): K0 make:easy acc:low. Rats and fleas are unremarkable. Clothes and bedding of the dead are suspected, rightly. Cheap and possible: flee early, shun coughing patients, boil or burn bedding, keep rats from grain. Local: grain stores at Orsanmichele; second-hand clothes dealers (rigattieri); wool and cloth warehouses.
- `scurvy_citrus` (Fresh food prevents scurvy (citrus, vitamin C)): K0 make:easy acc:medium. Galleys coast from port to port, so sea scurvy is rare; it appears in sieges and famine. Lemons, citrons and bitter oranges come from Sicily, Amalfi and Liguria.
- `typhus_lice` (Typhus carried by body lice (delousing)): K0 make:easy acc:low. Lice are universal and thought to breed from sweat and humours. Famine fevers of 1347 are not told apart. Boiling or baking clothes is possible wherever there is fuel.
- `vitamins_deficiency` (Deficiency diseases (beriberi, rickets, pellagra, goitre, night blindness)): K0 make:easy acc:low. Disease from a missing food is an alien idea. Goitre in Alpine and Apennine valleys is blamed on the water. Liver for night blindness is in the medical authorities.
- `blood_circulation` (Circulation of the blood): K0 make:medium acc:low. Galen: blood ebbs and flows, passes through pores in the heart wall. Silver is draining abroad, and the commune recoined the grosso in 1345 and 1347. Local: Zecca (mint); Arte del Cambio (money-changers). Elsewhere: Venice, the ducat; Genoa, the genovino.
- `division_of_labour` (Division of labour and specialisation): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Wool cloth passes through some two dozen trades under a merchant's direction; Villani counts over 200 workshops and 30,000 people living from it. Practised, never theorised. Local: Arte della Lana; Arte di Calimala (finishing imported cloth). Elsewhere: Venice, the Arsenal.
- `interest_loans_collateral` (Interest-bearing loans, pledges and limits on debt bondage): K4 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Open interest is the sin of usury. Bankers hide it in exchange rates and 'gifts' on deposits; Christian pawnbrokers pay a yearly fine and repent in their wills. Local: Arte del Cambio; licensed pawnbrokers; friar confessors.
- `partnership_commenda` (Risk-sharing partnership (commenda, mudaraba)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. Tuscan companies are partnerships renewed every few years, and every partner is liable with all he owns: the Bardi and Peruzzi partners are being stripped. Sea ventures use the commenda. Elsewhere: Genoa and Venice, commenda and colleganza.
- `public_debt_bonds` (Public debt and government bonds): K4 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. In 1343–45 the commune, unable to repay its forced loans, made them the Monte Comune: transferable 5 % credits. They trade below face; friars debate whether buying them is usury. Local: Monte Comune; officials of the Monte. Elsewhere: Venice, the Monte (since 1262); Genoa, the compere.
- `double_entry` (Double-entry bookkeeping): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Large Tuscan companies keep ledgers with matching debit and credit entries; layout and rigour vary, and small shops keep simple running accounts. No written manual exists. Local: ledgers of the merchant companies; abacus masters. Elsewhere: Genoa, communal treasury ledgers in full double entry (1340).
- `insurance` (Insurance (marine, fire, life)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Sea risk is covered by sea loans or by carriers who charge for taking the risk. A contract for a premium alone is new: the oldest known is Genoese, 1347. Local: merchant companies shipping through Porto Pisano. Elsewhere: Genoa, notaries drawing the first premium contracts.
- `price_mechanism_supply_demand` (Prices, supply and demand): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Merchants and friars know prices follow scarcity; a grain dealer recorded Orsanmichele's prices for years. In the 1346–47 dearth the commune fixed prices and hunted hoarders. Local: grain market at Orsanmichele; grain officials of the commune.
- `ever_normal_granary` (Public granaries and price stabilisation (ever-normal granary)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:high. In dearth the commune appoints grain officials who buy abroad and sell or bake at a loss, as in 1346–47. A standing reserve is not kept. Local: grain officials (ufficiali del biado); Orsanmichele (grain market and store). Elsewhere: Venice, public grain office; China, ever-normal granaries.
- `progressive_income_tax` (Income tax and progressive rates): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:low. The city pays through gate and sales taxes and forced loans, which bear interest; the property assessment (estimo), dropped in 1315, is hated. Only the contado pays by assessed wealth. Local: gabelle offices; Monte Comune. Elsewhere: Siena, taxes on surveyed property.
- `stock_exchange` (Stock exchange (securities market)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Brokers arrange exchange, goods and now Monte credits at the Mercato Nuovo. There are no fixed rules or posted prices. Local: Mercato Nuovo; brokers (sensali). Elsewhere: Bruges, merchants' exchange; Venice, Rialto.
- `comparative_advantage_free_trade` (Comparative advantage and free trade): K1 use:none make:easy acc:low. Policy is protection and privilege: guild monopolies, tolls, grain export bans and wars over routes to the sea. Florence lives by importing English wool and exporting cloth.
- `cooperatives_savings_banks` (Savings banks, credit and consumer cooperatives): K1 use:none make:easy acc:medium. Confraternities pool alms and guilds aid members. The poor borrow from pawnbrokers at high rates. No charitable pawn bank exists anywhere yet. Local: confraternities; Franciscans of Santa Croce.
- `quantity_theory_inflation` (Money supply, debasement and inflation): K1 use:none make:easy acc:medium. Everyone knows that debased coin buys less and that good coin is hoarded or exported. That the amount of money moves all prices is not a stated idea. Elsewhere: France, the king's repeated changes of the coinage.
- `joint_stock_company` (Joint-stock company and limited liability): K1 use:none make:medium acc:medium. No company has tradable shares or limited liability. Transferable Monte credits are the nearest thing. Ruined partners would see the point at once. Elsewhere: Genoa, the Maona of Chios (shareholders of the 1346 fleet, founded 1347); Toulouse, shares in the river mills.
- `paper_money` (Paper money): K1 use:none make:medium acc:low. Marco Polo describes the Khan's paper money, and Pegolotti tells merchants they must change silver for it in Cathay. After the bank failures nobody would trust a paper promise. Local: Pegolotti's Pratica della mercatura. Elsewhere: China, paper money under the Yuan (losing value).
- `national_accounts_gdp` (National income accounts (GDP)): K1 use:none make:hard acc:low. Villani's chapter on Florence around 1338 counts mouths, cloths, shops, schools and communal revenue: the nearest thing in Europe. Households fear any count as a new tax. Local: Giovanni Villani; gabelle offices; guild matriculation lists.
- `economic_growth_productivity` (Wealth as productivity; sustained economic growth): K0 make:easy acc:medium. Wealth means treasure, land and the city's share of trade. Florentines see fortune's wheel in the bank failures; output per head rising for good is unimagined.
- `aggregate_demand_countercyclical_policy` (Fighting slumps by sustaining demand (Keynesian policy)): K0 make:hard acc:low. Money is coin, credit has collapsed and the commune cannot pay its own debts. Work on the cathedral and campanile to employ the poor is understood as piety and charity.
- `central_bank` (Central bank and lender of last resort): K0 make:hard acc:low. No lender stood behind the failing banks; the commune itself was their debtor. The Monte manages debt, not credit. Elsewhere: Venice, Rialto transfer banks under state supervision.
- `life_tables_annuities` (Life tables and the pricing of annuities): K0 make:hard acc:medium. Northern towns sell life rents at one price for all ages. No record of deaths by age exists; the baptistery counts only births. Elsewhere: Flemish and north French towns, life rents.

## Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`) — [deep tech links](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/catalog/military.md)
- `cavalry_chariot` (Horse warfare (chariot, cavalry, horse archers)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. The armoured man-at-arms is the core of every army; Florence hires German and other mercenary horse. Hungarian mounted archers ride through Italy with King Louis in 1347–48.
- `crossbow_longbow` (Bows of war (composite bow, crossbow, longbow)): K4 use:correct make:easy acc:high. The crossbow is the standard missile weapon of foot, walls and galleys. News of Crécy (1346) says English longbows outshot the hired Genoese crossbowmen. Local: crossbow makers; crossbowmen of the commune. Elsewhere: Genoa, crossbowmen for hire; England, longbow; Hungarians and Mongols, composite bow.
- `mercenaries_citizen_militia` (Mercenaries, militias and the loyalty of armed men): K4 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Florence fights with hired foreign cavalry and fears it: Werner of Urslingen's Great Company plundered Tuscany in 1342. The guild militia mans walls and won the street fights of 1343. Local: the sixteen militia companies (gonfaloni); wartime commissions of citizens. Elsewhere: the Great Company, in 1347–48 with Louis of Hungary's army.
- `torsion_artillery_trebuchet` (Mechanical artillery (torsion catapult, trebuchet)): K4 use:correct make:medium acc:high. Counterweight trebuchets are the siege artillery of the day, built on the spot by master carpenters. Ancient torsion engines are known only from Vegetius and Vitruvius. Local: master carpenters and engineers hired by the commune.
- `oared_galley_ram` (Oared war galley and ram tactics): K4 use:partial make:hard acc:medium. Galleys fight by boarding and crossbows; no rams, no guns. Florence has no fleet or port of its own and hires or allies for ships. Local: Pisa and Porto Pisano. Elsewhere: Venice Arsenal; Genoa; Catalan and Angevin fleets.
- `collective_security_alliances` (Alliances and collective security): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. The Guelf cities of Tuscany and Naples make leagues with fixed contingents of horse. Allies arrive late or make separate peace. Elsewhere: Naples, the Angevin crown (Queen Joanna, invaded 1347–48); Perugia, Siena, Bologna: Guelf allies.
- `field_fortification` (Field fortification (marching camp, wagon fort, entrenchment)): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Armies camp behind ditches and palisades, and besiegers build fortified camps (bastie). Levied peasants dig. Reports say the English at Crécy fought from a prepared position.
- `siegecraft_mining` (Siegecraft, mining and counter-mining): K3 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Sieges are won by blockade, trebuchets, timber-propped mines, treachery and hunger. Calais held out eleven months against Edward III (1346–47). Elsewhere: Calais, the English siege.
- `cannon_artillery` (Cannon and artillery): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Florence ordered metal guns and iron balls in 1326. Guns are few and small, frightening more than breaching; walls fall to trebuchets and hunger. Villani reports English guns at Crécy. Local: bell founders; the commune's gun masters. Elsewhere: Calais, English guns at the siege (1346–47); China, bronze and iron cannon.
- `gunpowder` (Gunpowder (black powder)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Known to a few specialists and from Latin recipe books; made in small amounts as a loose meal. Saltpetre is scarce and dear, bought through Venice or from apothecaries. Local: apothecaries (Arte dei Medici e Speziali); masters of the commune's guns. Elsewhere: China, powder weapons of many kinds; Mamluk Egypt and Syria.
- `military_engineering_roads_bridges` (Military engineering (roads, bridges, pioneers)): K3 use:partial make:medium acc:high. The commune hires master masons and carpenters as engineers for each campaign; labour is levied peasants. No permanent corps. Local: masters of the Opera del Duomo and the city walls. Elsewhere: Paris, Guido da Vigevano (book of siege devices, 1335).
- `balance_of_power` (Balance of power): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Cities league against whoever grows too strong, as Florence and Venice did against Mastino della Scala (1336–39). Party labels, Guelf and Ghibelline, still cut across such reasoning. Local: Parte Guelfa; ambassadors of the commune. Elsewhere: Milan, the Visconti; Verona, the della Scala.
- `deterrence` (Deterrence): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Leagues, walls and hired companies are kept to discourage attack. Against free companies the usual answer is to pay them to go elsewhere.
- `laws_of_war` (Laws of war (humanitarian law)): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Theologians teach the just war. Knights are taken for ransom, peasants plundered, and a town taken by storm may be sacked. Free companies respect only payment. Elsewhere: Crécy 1346, few prisoners taken; Calais 1347, the burghers' surrender.
- `military_camp_hygiene` (Camp hygiene and army health): K2 use:none make:easy acc:medium. Vegetius, read in Bono Giamboni's Tuscan, advises clean water and moving camp. In practice siege camps rot, and camp fevers are blamed on bad air. Elsewhere: Caffa 1346, plague in the besieging Mongol army; Calais 1346–47, sickness in the English camp.
- `military_intelligence_codebreaking` (Military intelligence and codebreaking): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:high. Merchants' letters are the best intelligence in Europe. Secret writing is simple: cover names and a few substituted letters. Nobody in Italy analyses ciphers systematically. Local: chancery of the Signoria; merchant company correspondents. Elsewhere: Avignon, papal chancery code lists; Mamluk chancery, Arabic treatises on breaking ciphers.
- `strategy_theory` (Strategy as a subject of study): K2 use:partial make:easy acc:medium. Vegetius and Frontinus are the authorities, Vegetius also in Tuscan. Italian wars aim at ravaging, ransom and negotiated peace; captains avoid pitched battle. Local: Bono Giamboni's Tuscan Vegetius; chancery of the Signoria.
- `chemical_weapons` (Poison gas and its prohibition): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:low. Stinking smoke in mines and breaches is an accepted trick. Poison is dishonourable, and in 1348 a rumour of poisoning is enough to get people killed.
- `close_order_infantry` (Disciplined close-order infantry (phalanx, legion)): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. The guild militia fights on foot with shields, spears and crossbows but is little drilled; hired cavalry decides campaigns. Vegetius is read in Tuscan. Foot have lately beaten knights abroad. Local: the sixteen militia companies (gonfaloni). Elsewhere: Swiss confederates (Laupen 1339); Flanders (Courtrai 1302); England, dismounted men-at-arms with archers (Crécy 1346).
- `incendiaries_greek_fire` (Incendiary weapons and Greek fire): K2 use:partial make:medium acc:medium. Fire arrows and pots of pitch, sulphur and oil are used in sieges and at sea. Byzantine Greek fire is a legend.
- `conscription_mass_army` (Conscription and the mass army): K2 use:partial make:hard acc:low. Every citizen owes militia service in his company, and the contado sends foot and diggers. Rich men pay substitutes; long campaigns are left to mercenaries.
- `standing_army_logistics` (Standing army, pay and supply): K2 use:none make:hard acc:low. The commune hires companies by short contract for each war and dismisses them at peace; paying soldiers in peacetime looks like tyranny and waste. Roman legions are known from books. Elsewhere: Mamluk Egypt, a standing slave army; Venice, a permanent fleet and arsenal.
- `security_dilemma_arms_race` (Security dilemma and arms races): K1 use:none make:easy acc:medium. Lived daily between Florence, Pisa, Lucca, Milan and Verona and described in council speeches, never as a general principle.
- `arms_control` (Arms control and disarmament agreements): K1 use:none make:medium acc:low. Leagues fix how many troops each ally must send, never limits. Inside the walls statutes ban carrying weapons and cap tower heights. The church's old ban on crossbows is ignored.
- `ballistics_gunnery` (Ballistics and scientific gunnery): K1 use:none make:medium acc:medium. Engineers range trebuchets by trial. Theory says a missile flies straight until its impressed force is spent, then falls. Elsewhere: Paris, Buridan's impetus theory.
- `handguns_muskets` (Handguns and muskets (matchlock, flintlock)): K1 use:none make:medium acc:medium. No hand-held firearm is in service in Italy; the few guns are fixed pieces. Small hand guns appear in Italian records only in the 1360s. Elsewhere: China, metal hand cannon since the late 13th century.
- `war_rockets` (War rockets): K1 use:none make:medium acc:low. Latin recipe books mention 'flying fire'; no Italian army uses it and no fireworks are shown at feasts yet. Elsewhere: China, rockets in war.
- `wargaming_operations_research` (War games and operations research): K0 make:easy acc:medium. Chess is the only war game, played keenly in Florence. Counting what actually worked would appeal to merchants who audit everything else.
- `bastion_fortification` (Bastioned fortification (trace italienne)): K0 make:hard acc:low. Guns do not yet threaten walls, so nobody sees the need. Defence means height: Florence's new circuit (finished 1333) has tall thin curtains and towers. Local: third circle of walls (1284–1333).
- `general_staff_war_college` (General staff and war college): K0 make:hard acc:low. War is run by a temporary commission of citizens and a hired captain with his household. The Twenty who ran the Lucca war (1341) are remembered for waste and corruption.
- `pike_and_shot_drill` (Pike and shot, volley fire and drill): K0 make:hard acc:low. Neither handguns nor drilled pike blocks exist here. Drill by word of command needs men kept under pay all year, which no commune does.
